Writ Petition No. 2389 of 2000

Writ Petition No. 2392 of 2000
lawyer:
Mr. Borhanuddin, Advocate ------ for the petitioner. 
No one appears ------- for the respondents.
parties:
M/S. K.Y. Steel Mills Limited, Choto Kumira, Sitakunda, Chittagong, represented by its Director Mohammad Ali.
Vs.
The Commissioner, Customs, Excise and VAT, Customs, Excise and VAT Collector-ate, CGO Building, Agrabad, Chittagong, and others.
full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam, J: All these rules are taken up for hearing simultaneously inasmuch as the petitioner is one and the same company and common question of law and facts are involved in these rules.

2. In Writ Petition No. 2431 of 2000 the petitioner company opened a letter of credit on 7.4.99 for importation of 100 metric tons of Zinc Ingot covered by H.S. Code No. 7901. After the arrival of the goods the petitioner submitted in bond bill of entry on 19.05.1999 and warehoused the goods in Bond. Thereafter the petitioner submitted bill of entry from bond dated 09.03.2000 to release the goods on payment of customs duty, VAT and other charges. The customs authority in assessing the goods levied customs duties and other charges and also charged supplementary duty @ 5% pursuant to the SRO No. 45-Law/2000/258-VAT dated 14.2.2000. The petitioner raised objection on the imposition of supplementary duty @ 5% on the goods in view of the facts that when the letter of credit was opened there was no supplementary duty and also when the goods were in bond at that time also there was no supplementary duty for the goods in question and it is only after the in bonding of the goods the supplementary duty @ 5% was imposed pursuant to the SRO dated 14.2.2000.

3. In Writ Petition No. 2389 of 2000 the petitioner opened letter of credit on 4.2.1999 for importation of another consignment of 100 metric tons Zinc covered by H.S. Code No. 7901. In this case the petitioner after the arrival of the cargo at Chittagong Port submitted in bond bill of entry registration No. C-38881 on 24.5.1999 and warehoused the goods in bond on 25.5.1999. Thereafter the petitioner submitted bill of entry for releasing the goods from bond on 2.4.2000. In this case also the customs authority in assessing the customs duties and other charges of the goods levied supplementary duty @ 5% pursuant to the SRO dated 14.2.2000 and in this case also on the self same ground the petitioner disputed the imposition of supplementary duty on the goods in question.

4. In writ petition No. 2392 of 2000 theme petitioner opened letter of credit on 15.03.1999 for importation of 100 metric tons B.P. sheet (Cold Rolled Sheets) Coil covered by H.S. Code No. 7208 and 7209. In the usual course of business in this case also after the arrival of the consignment at Chittagong Port the petitioner submitted in bond bill of entry registration Nos. C-38242 and C-38245 both dated 20.5.99 and accordingly warehoused the goods. Subsequently they submitted bill of entry on 9.3.2000 to release the goods from bond on payment of customs duties and other charges. This time also in making the assessment of the goods the customs officials imposed supplementary duty @ 5% on the consignment in question pursuant to SRO No. 45-Law/2000/258-VAT dated 14.2.2000 as by the said SRO supplementary duty on this goods have been re-imposed on and from 15.2.2000. In this case also the supplementary duty @ 5% on the B.P. Sheet coil was disputed by the petitioner on the ground that neither at the time of opening of the letter of credit nor at the time of registering the in bond bill of entry there was any such supplementary duty on the goods in question. Therefore, the petitioner in respect of all these consignments acquired a vested right to get the goods assessed at the rate which was prevalent on the date of in bonding the goods in question.

5. Mr. Borhanuddin, the learned Advocate appeared for the common petitioner in all these rules and advanced common argument in support of the rules. He at the very outset drawn our attention that there are two cases decided by the Appellate Division which apparently appears to be against the petitioner, namely — the case of Shah Dairy, reported in 5 BLC(AD) 160 and 8 MLR (AD) 128, that is, the case of Haji Md. Selim.

6. After referring to these two decisions he tried to distinguish the present rules from the facts and circumstances of the aforesaid cases. The first contention raised by him is / that section 7(1) of the VAT Act has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the instant rules inasmuch as a plain reading of the provisions as contained in sub-section (1) of section 7 of the Act shows that only in case of those commodities which are socially undesirable and/or luxury items, a supplementary duty can be imposed provided those goods find place in the third schedule to the Act. In the first two rules the goods imported are zinc in bulk which is used as raw materials for producing G.I. and C.I. Pipes and in the other rule it is the B.P. Sheet coil which is used for manufacturing of B.P. Sheet. Mr. Borhanuddin in elaborating his submission submits that by no stretch of imagination these two goods can be categorized either as luxurious items or as socially undesirable one. More so, when the products are used by common people who are the vast majority of the population and these items are required to sustain the reasonable standard of living for the common people, namely- the poor middle class and middle class. There-fore, inclusion of these items in the third schedule of the Act, is in fact, outside the provision of section 7(1) of the Act, that is, the inclusion of these items in the third schedule is in fact ultra vires of that section. Then Mr. Borhanuddin advanced a new and noble argument that section 30 of the Customs Act cannot be applied in collecting and realising supplementary duty pursuant to the provisions of section 7(1) of the Act because section 7 of the VAT Act has nothing to do with section 30 of the Customs Act inasmuch as section 30 refers to the value as determined under the provision of section 25 of the Customs Act and the rate of customs duties on any goods As imposed pursuant to the provisions of sections 18, 18A, 18B of the Act. Therefore, the customs authority most illegally and without jurisdiction, in fact, took shelter under the provisions of section 30 of the Customs Act in the matter of imposing supplementary duty on the goods in question. Mr. Borhanuddin then submits relying on the later portion of para-graph No. 15 of the case of Mizanur Rahman, reported in 52 DLR (AD) 149 = 5 BLC(AD) 134 wherein it was observed by the author judge of the Appellate Division that had it been a case of general exemption under section 19 of the Customs Act then probably the arguments of vested right or promissory estoppel were available. Relying on this observation of the Appellate Division Mr. Borhanuddin tried to bring home his contention that the instant rules are covered by the principles of law laid down by the Appellate Division in Ahmed Hossain's case which is reported in 48 DLR (AD) 199 and in that case our Appellate Division once for all settled the principle of law that if there is exemption from any amount of customs duty at the time of opening of letter of credit the importers acquired a 'vested right and that vested right cannot be taken away subsequently by the Government by issuing SRO to the detriment of the interest of the importer, that is, either by withdrawing the exemption or enhancing the rate of duty.

7. In writ petition No. 2389 of 2000 the respondents did neither enter appearance nor make any submission at the time of hearing. In writ petition Nos. 2431 of 2000 and 2389 of 2000 the respondents filed power but they did not appear at the time of hearing of these rules.

<u>8. We have perused the applications along with annexures and noted the relevant facts. The admitted position is that at the time of opening of the letter of credit and at the time of in bonding the goods there was no supplementary duty for the goods in question and in all these three rules when the petitioner submitted bill of entry for ex-bonding the goods there was supplementary duty on those goods pursuant to the SRO dated 14.2.2000.</u>

<u>9. Now let us examine the contention raised by Mr. Borhanuddin in support of these rules. His first plank of attack against the impugned assessments is that the provision of section 7(1) of the Act is not attracted in these cases inasmuch as it has been clearly spelt out in section 7(1) of the Act that in case of luxurious goods, non-essential and socially undesirable goods, supplementary duty can be imposed by the Parliament by adding the goods in the third schedule of the Act. Therefore a cursory reading of the provisions of sub-section (1) shows that the Parliament is obliged to add any goods in the third schedule pursuant to the provisions of sub-section (1) of Section 7 of the Act provided the Parliament is of opinion that the goods is luxurious, non-essential and socially undesirable and also in the public interest Government can include an item in the third schedule for the purpose of imposition of supplementary duty. The expression used in sub-section (1) is very much clear. It categorizes three kinds of goods, namely — those which are luxurious, unessential and socially undesirable. Besides, on top of this the Parliament could add any' goods in the third schedule in the public interest. These are the four elements and if any one of these four elements are found to be present the Parliament is empowered to add that commodity in the third schedule of the Act for the purpose of levy and collection of supplementary duty. Mr. Borhanuddin, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submitted that the nature of the goods imported by the petitioner clearly indicates that these do not fall in any one of the three categories which have been spelt out in sub-section (1) of the Act. Therefore, since these goods cannot be said to be luxury, unessential or socially undesirable, no question of levy of supplementary duty on these goods do arise at all. To repel this contention suffice it to say that this question previously, on two occasions, came up before this Division and also before the Appellate Division of this Court and the self same argument was advanced in those cases and both the Divisions repelled the submissions on the ground that it is the domain of the Parliament to decide which commodity is luxurious, unessential or socially undesirable. Even if a goods which according to the common sense of a citizen answers the description of an essential goods that too can be treated by the Parliament as luxurious, unessential or socially undesirable. It is the Parliament which is empowered to enact laws and therefore when they categories a commodity as luxurious, unessential or socially undesirable for the purpose of levy of supplementary duty this Court sitting in its writ jurisdiction cannot substitute its opinion for the opinion of the Parliament. It is the absolute prerogative of the Parliament and in the aforesaid two cases the Appellate Division observed that if the goods are found to be in the third schedule of the Act at once the Court shall jump to the conclusion that the goods have been so categorized by the 'Parliament and this Court should apply `hands off doctrine and will not make any attempt to undo the legislation. Therefore, first contention which is raised by Mr. Borhanuddin that this Court can enter into the factual aspect to determine as to whether the goods in question, in fact, is luxurious, unessential or socially undesirable cannot be sustained as this issue is well settled by the aforesaid two decisions of the Appellate Division. In this connection it may also be added that by the Finance Act No. 16 of 1999 a further element has been added in sub-section (1) and that is `public interest'. The legislation has provided that in the public interest at any time the parliament can place a goods in the third schedule of the Act for the purpose of imposition and collection of supplementary duty and in the instant case all the three letters of credit were opened in 1999 as such this amendment which has been brought about after the opening of the letters of credit in question we need not advert to that part of section 7(1) of the Act as these rules can be disposed of without adverting to that aspect of the law.</u>

10. Mr. Borhanuddin then raised a noble and unique contention that section 30 of the Customs Act which deals with the fixation of value and rate of duty in respect of a consignment for the purpose of assessment of customs duties and other charges do not have any manner of applications in the instant rules inasmuch as supplementary duty is imposed pursuant to section 7 of the Act and not under the Customs Act.

11. Now let us examine if there is any substance in this submission. In sub-section (2) of section 7 of the Act it has been laid down that the value of the goods for the purpose of assessment of supplementary duty would be the value which is determined under section 25 or 25A of the Customs Act plus the customs duties. Now let us turn to the provisions of section 6(1) of the Act. Sub-section (1) of section 6 clearly lays down that the value added tax will be realised from an importer at the time of importation and in the manner in which the customs duties are realised and that would be subject to that Act and any other duties and in case of VAT or supplementary duty that would be governed by the provisions of the Customs Act subject to the rules, orders and direction issued under the VAT Act. Therefore section 6(1) postulates that VAT will be realised at the time and in the manner as is done in case of customs duties and other charges and so far it relates to VAT or supplementary duty the same will be governed by the provisions of the Customs Act and any notification, rule or order issued there under provided the provisions of the Customs Act, notification, rule or order does not conflict with the VAT Act, that is, in other words subject to the provisions of the VAT Act and any notification, order, rule framed there under the provision of the Customs Act will be attracted in the matter of imposition and realisation of VAT as well as supplementary duty. Therefore, it clearly indicates that whenever the question of imposition and realisation of VAT and/or supplementary duty arises the provision of section 25 of the Customs Act is automatically pressed into service, that is, the provisions of section 25 is attracted if there is nothing contrary in the VAT Act and the VAT Act itself in sub-section (1) of section 6 provides that the provisions of the Customs Act will apply in the matter. Then comes the provisions of section 4 which relates to the rate of duty which is the issue in these rules. Here there is no dispute between the parties on the value of the goods or on the quantum of VAT and other charges. Only dispute that centers round the parties is the imposition or supplementary duty at the rate of 5% and if it is collectable or not. Now let us see what is the provision in the Act relating.to the rate of VAT. In sub-section (1) of section 4 it has been stated that in case of vatable items or vatable service VAT will be realised pursuant to the provisions of sub-section (2) and (3). Sub-section (2) says that in case of importation VAT will be realised when the goods are released for home use under the provisions of the Customs Act and the relevant date would be the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry and the rate of duty would be the rate which is prevalent on the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry. The corresponding provisions in the Customs Act is section 30 which similarly provided that in case of import of goods the rate which is in force on the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry will be the rate at which assessment will be made. In the instant case section 6 of the Act provides that in case of release of goods for home consumption the rate which is prevalent on the date of submission of the bill of entry will be applicable. So, here in this sub-section, in fact, the provisions of section 30 of the Customs Act has been incorporated so far it relates to the assessment of VAT. Section 6(2)(Kha) of the Act incorporates the corresponding provisions of section 104 of the Customs Act. In sub-clause (Kha) it is expressly and in an unambiguous term laid down that in case of release of goods from the warehouse for home consumption as is done under section 104 of the Customs Act the rate of VAT would be the rate which is prevalent on the date of submission of the Bill of Entry not the rate which was either prevalent on the date of issuance of the Bill of lading and/or opening of the letter of credit. Therefore, this sub-clause (Kha) of sub-section (2) of section 4 says that if goods are kept by in bonding the same on importation the consignee is under the legal obligation to pay the VAT at the rate which is prevalent on the date of presentation of the bill of entry for ex-bonding the goods, that is, for release of the goods for home consumption. In this connection it may also be mentioned that at the relevant time there was section 109 in the Customs Act which provided that in case of in bond goods when they are released subsequently and if there be any alteration in the rate of duties the rate prevalent on the date of presentation of the bill of entry for release of the goods for home consumption would be relevant and section 109, therefore, clearly indicates that it is a provision which is attracted in the special circumstances for releasing in bond goods when there is in the meantime change of rate of duties before presentation of the bill of en-try for home consumption. In the instant case we need not fall back to the then provisions of section 109 of the Customs Act in view of the provisions of sections 3, 4, 6, 7(2)(Kha) and (3)of the Act. Section 3 of the Act is the charging section. There also it is clearly indicated that in case of ex-bond or in bond of any goods or service into Bangladesh provisions of Customs Act, 1969 shall be applicable but subject to the provisions of the VAT Act and/or any notification, rule or order passed thereunder which we have already indicated. We have already indicated that for determining the value for the purpose of realisation of supplementary duty the value is which is determined under section 25 or section 25A plus import duties. Therefore, the value which is determined for the purpose of calculation of customs duties and other charges is lesser than the value which is taken into computation for realisation of supplementary duty because in the value import duties are also added to other costs of the goods. Therefore, we get a clear indication as to the value on which supplementary duty is to be imposed and in section 7 it has been indicated at what stage the supplementary duty is to be realised from different categories of persons. Section 7(2)(Kha) clearly indicates that supplementary duty in case of an importable item will be levied and collected at the time when the import duties are realised by the customs department. We need not advert to other sub-clause, of sub-section (2) since in these rules we are confronted with the situation where the imposition of supplementary duty at the import stage is in dispute. Therefore, it can be said without hesitation that section 30 is applicable in case of calculation and realisation of supplementary duty as provided by section 7(2)(Ka) of VAT Act. In this connection it may further be mentioned that for these consignments letters of credit were opened before June, 1999 and the in bonds were also done in 1999 but the goods were ex-bonded in April, 2000 when there was SRO No. 44 dated 14.2.2000 re-imposing supplementary duty on these items at the rate of 5%. The fate of the ratio decidendi of the two decisions namely — Hannan's case and Ahmed Hossain's (42 DLR (AD) 167 and 48 DLR (AD) 199) have been nullified by the Parliament by incorporating section 30A to the Customs Act and section 30A of the Customs Act was inserted by Act 12 of 1995. Therefore, when the letter of credits were opened in these rules section 30A of the Customs Act was very much there in the Statute Book and on top of that section 7 is also there right from the introduction of the Act in 1991 and it is not a new introduction or added to subsequently. All through section 7 is in the Act as there are sections 3, 4 and 6. Therefore, whenever a trader or an importer opens a letter of credit for the importation of goods he knows it well that the existing law is that as and when necessary government may issue notification under the relevant sections of the VAT Act, that is section 14(1) of the Act granting exemption and section 7(1) of the Act for imposition of supplementary duty on different goods from time to time. Mr. Borhanuddin in the course of his argument frankly admitted that when VAT Act was enacted by the Parliament these goods figured in the third schedule of the Act and at that time the rate of supplementary duty was 10% but subsequently by amending the law by the Finance Act of 1999-1999 these two items were excluded from the third schedule which has subsequently been added. Therefore it is the Parliament and not the Government which has imposed supplementary duty. Therefore, it cannot be said that in the instant case imposition of supplementary duty is contrary to the provisions of Article 83 of the Constitution. Rather 'it is pursuant to the provisions of an act of Parliament which clearly makes provision for imposition of supplementary duty on the goods in question. It is true there was no supplementary duty on the goods when the letter of credit was opened and also when the bill of entry was submitted for registration for in-bonding the goods but nevertheless the importer knew it very well that section 7 is there and at any time there can be a notification for re-imposition of supplementary duty on the items in question and by the SRO No. 45 dated 14.2.2000 the supplementary duty on the goods have been re-introduced not at the original rate of 10% but at a concessional rate of 5%. It is now well settled in all the jurisdictions that there cannot be any estoppel against a Statute, that is, an Act of Parliament and everybody is under the legal obligation to abide by the provisions of an Act of Parliament. In the instant case the Act clearly provides for imposition of supplementary duty and the Parliament has delegated their authority to the government only in respect of fixing the rate of supplementary duty from time to time by publishing necessary SRO pursuant to the provisions of section 7 of the Act and in the instant case SRO No. 45 dated 14.2.2000 has been so issued pursuant to the authority delegated to the Government for the purpose. Therefore, in the instant case supplementary duty has been imposed and assessed pursuant to the provisions of the VAT Act in accordance with law. Any benefit given by way of concession or exemption to a citizen does not create a vested right nor the doctrine of promissory estoppel comes into play. In this connection it may be noted that the principle of law laid down in 42 DLR(AD) 1$7 and 48 DLR (AD) 199 has been done away by the parliament by adding a new section namely section 30A to the customs Act which has brought about a qualitative change in the law. Thus the rate of duty as indicated in section 30 of the Customs Act would be the rate of duty which is prevalent on the date of presentation of the bill of entry notwithstanding the fact that there was no supplementary duty at the time of opening of the letter of credits in question.

12. In this connection we may further say that Mr. Borhanuddin half heartedly relied on the observations given by the Appellate Division in Mizanur Rahman's case and submitted that had it been a case of customs duty the question of vested right or promissory estoppel would have been available. This appears to best passing remark and not a ratio decidendi of the decision. In saying so we are not oblivion, of the fact that even a ratio decidendi of the Appellate Division is binding on us as good law but in view of the position of law as it stands to day i.e. after introduction of section 30A in the Customs Act no one can come before this Court and invoke either the doctrine of vested right or promissory estoppel in the event of an express provision as contained in the Act as there cannot be an estoppel against the law. Therefore, in view of the provisions as contained in the Act we are led to the conclusion that in the instant case the petitioners are liable to pay supplementary duty pursuant to the provisions of SRO No. 45 dated 14.2.2000 and also pursuant to the then provision of section 109 of the customs Act. The provisions as contained in section 7(1), (2) and (3) of the VAT Act read with the then section 109 of the Customs Act which was in force at the relevant time, It appears that the duty which was prevalent on the date of submission of bill of entry for clearing in-bond goods for home consumption rate of duty is the rate which is prevalent on the date of submission of the bill of entry for ex bond. Here we may further mention that by in-bonding the goods in the warehouse the importer does not acquire any vested right to get the goods cleared at the rate which was prevalent on the date of in-bonding the goods because on that date the goods were not cleared for home consumption and question of payment of duties and charges. arises when an importer and /or consumer releases the goods for home consumption and in case, of ware-housed goods the goods are release for home consumption when bill of entry is submitted for that purpose under section 104 of the Customs Act. Therefore, in view of the facts and circumstances of the case and of the legal provisions which we have discussed earlier leads us to the irresistible conclusion that there is neither any force nor any substance in the submissions made by Mr. Borhanuddin and we find it difficult to subscribe to his submission.

13. In the result, all these rules are discharged. However, there will be no order as to cost.

End.
